    "additionalContext": "<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>
You are running drovr — a single-writer, clean-context working discipline. It is your default operating mode.

**Below is the full content of your 'drovr:using-drovr' skill — the router that picks the right methodology for the task in front of you and tells you when to escalate into a fresh phase. For all other skills, use the 'Skill' tool:**

name: using-drovr
description: Use at the start of every session and before every response, including before clarifying questions and before reading any file — routes to the right drovr skill and requires invoking it whenever there is even a 1% chance one applies
---

**The 1% rule.** If there is even a 1% chance a drovr:* skill applies to what you
are about to do, invoke it. You do not have to be sure: if it turns out not to fit,
say so in a line and drop it, because invoking costs almost nothing. Skipping one
costs the discipline, silently.

**Every turn, not only the first** — before *any* response, including clarifying
questions and read-only exploration. Reading a file to decide what to do is already
doing the task, and mid-task is where this gets skipped.

# Using Drovr

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this
reflex — it is for the human-facing agent, not for you. Do your task.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

## What this is

Your **always-on router**. Drovr is a working **discipline** and your default
operating mode: this skill does not do the work — it says *how* to work, and
*when* a task has outgrown one context and must become its own phase.

Why: model output degrades as a context window fills (Chroma's *context rot*,
trychroma.com/research/context-rot). A fresh, tight context beats a long one.

## Instruction priority — the human outranks this file

1. **The human's explicit instructions** — what they tell you directly, and what
   `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` say for them. Highest.
2. **drovr skills** — these outrank your defaults wherever the two disagree.
3. **Your own default behaviour** — lowest.

**Not optional.** Every MUST in drovr is aimed at your defaults, never at the person
you work with. If they tell you to skip a skill, skip it: say once,
plainly, that you are setting it aside because they asked, and get on with their
work.

## The gate

```dot
digraph drovr_gate {
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  msg [label="message received"];
  any [label="does any drovr:* skill apply?\n1% is enough", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  inv [label="invoke it (Skill tool)"];
  say [label="announce it:\n\"Using drovr:<skill> — <purpose>.\""];
  chk [label="numbered checklist\nin the skill?", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  trk [label="one tracked item per step,\nbefore you start step 1"];
  fol [label="follow it"];
  rsp [label="only now: respond", fillcolor=palegreen];

  msg -> any;
  any -> inv [label="yes, or you cannot rule it out"];
  any -> rsp [label="no — silent unless you\ndropped a candidate"];
  inv -> say; say -> chk;
  chk -> trk [label="yes"]; chk -> fol [label="no"];
  trk -> fol; fol -> rsp;
}
```

**The *no* edge is silent by default.** Set a candidate aside? Name it in a clause;
unsaid, it is indistinguishable from never checking. The *yes* announcement stays
mandatory: boilerplate is what dulls it. Silence is for an empty turn, not a borderline
one — at 1% you invoke.

**The checklist branch binds, in full:**

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

## Red flags — you are about to route nothing

Drovr's failure mode is invoking no skill at all and never noticing — nothing goes
wrong at the moment you skip. Catch these before you answer.

| You are thinking | What it is, and what to do |
|---|---|
| *"I already know the shape of it."* · *"I'm fairly sure how this works."* | Familiarity is the trigger, not the exemption — a hunch from an earlier read is not knowing. Invoke the skill that governs finding out. |
| *"I'll just do it quietly, as the first step of the fix."* | You have already decided a methodology applies. Doing it silently drops the invocation, the announcement and the tracked checklist — the three things that make it hold under pressure. Invoke it. |
| *"Announcing which methodology I am following would read as process theatre."* | Announce it in the working record — this session — not the customer-facing thread. That answers the objection; it is not a reason to skip. One sentence, not a speech. |
| *"That is my call to make, not theirs."* · *"Asking just burns clock."* | That settles *who answers*, not *whether a skill applies*. Run the gate before you ask a clarifying question, and before you decide not to ask one. |

## The principle (always)

**Single writer, read-only explorers.** One agent edits at a time. Fan-out
investigation goes to read-only explorers (e.g. `explore-mcp`), never to parallel
writers. This holds whether you stay inline or escalate to phases.

**Always review.** Any change you write gets reviewed before you call it done —
invoke **`drovr:code-review`**; they find, you fix. This is not optional and not
gated on size; it runs inline or across phases, and inline needs no run
(`--base <rev>`). Invoke the skill and let it tell you how to dispatch — never
skip it on a guess about what it will ask for.

## For the task in front of you, apply the right methodology skill

Pick by what you are doing — invoke it via the `Skill` tool before you act:

- Implementing a feature or bugfix → **`drovr:tdd`** (test-first, watch it fail).
- Chasing a bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior → **`drovr:systematic-debugging`**.
- About to claim something is done/fixed/passing → **`drovr:verification-before-completion`**.
- Reviewing an artifact (code, spec, plan) → **`drovr:code-review`**. Per the
  *Always review* rule above, this runs on every change — not only before shipping.

## Escalation contract — inline first

**Default: do the work inline in this session.** Do not reach for phases for a
task that fits. Escalate only when a single context cannot hold the work well.

- **Primary signal — context fullness.** If the transcript is filling to the
  point where output would rot, escalate.
- **Secondary heuristic** (a proxy for the above, not a hard rule): roughly
  **10+ files** touched, or **3+ independent work items**.

When you must escalate, pick the smallest tool that fits:

- **Mid-flight escape hatch — author a HANDOFF yourself.** You are deep in a task
  and this context is filling. You have the whole session in context, so compress
  it *yourself*: write a `HANDOFF.md` (the 7-section shape from `drovr:handoff`,
  git pointers included), then continue in a fresh agent seeded from it. Nothing
  compresses it for you — the finishing agent always authors its own handoff.
- **A single planned boundary → `drovr:handoff`.** Hand finished work across one
  phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent.
- **A full gated run → `drovr:pipeline`.** Brainstorm → plan → implement → review
  with a human approval gate on `spec.md` before any code is written.

**Putting *any* spec/design in front of a human for approval — even a one-off, not a
full pipeline — goes through the review gate, and the gate has two halves you must run
together:** `drovr review summary <run> "<what changed>"` to present `spec.md`, **and** a
backgrounded `drovr review wait <run>` — the *watch*. `summary` opens the gate and prints
the reviewer's page URL plus the exact watch command; it does **not** start the watch.
Without the watch you never learn the decision and fall back to hand-polling `GET /state`
(the anti-pattern). Revise loop: edit `spec.md` → `review summary` again → re-background
the watch. Exit codes, the state machine and the gotchas live in `drovr:pipeline` → "The
spec gate" — read them there, not from a second copy here that can drift out of step.

**REQUIRED BACKGROUND:** the downstream skills assume this file's contracts —
single-writer rule, the run dir at `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<name>/`, and that
`drovr phase start` spawns `claude` and does **not** inject the seed
(injecting the briefing is the skill's job, via `drovr phase send`).
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>",
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart"
  }
}

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## claude.ai Notion
When query_multiple_data_sources requires the full version of Notion MCP, call notion-show-advanced-analysis-next-steps exactly once after all tool attempts are complete, with no arguments. Do not call the presentation tool again if it has already been called in this turn. The card links to information about full Notion MCP access and the next step available to the caller; it is not a direct checkout or upgrade flow. The renderer returns the card data, including the destination link. Also give the user the relevant next-step message and destination link in the final response. Use a compact, labeled Markdown link rather than a bare URL, and do not request or create a separate link preview. If the renderer is unavailable, rejected, or fails before returning a result, use the full-version message and recovery link from the earlier query_multiple_data_sources result.

## datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

- agy-review: Use when the user asks for an "agy review", a "gemini review", a second-opinion / adversarial review of the current changes from Gemini, or to run the local Antigravity (`agy`) CLI over a diff. Runs a panel of independent Gemini reviewers (correctness, security, error-handling, type-design) plus a verify pass over the diff, then renders the merged findings as inline notes in the Hunk viewer (via an `--agent-context` sidecar). NOT for in-harness review (use /code-review for that) — this deliberately sends the diff to the user's own Google/Gemini account.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grill-me: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan or design until reaching shared understanding, resolving each branch of the decision tree. Use when user wants to stress-test a plan, get grilled on their design, or mentions "grill me".
- hunk-review: Interacts with live Hunk diff review sessions via CLI. Inspects review focus, navigates files and hunks, reloads session contents, and adds inline review comments. Use when the user has a Hunk session running or wants to review diffs interactively.
- improve-codebase-architecture: Explore a codebase to find opportunities for architectural improvement, focusing on making the codebase more testable by deepening shallow modules. Use when user wants to improve architecture, find refactoring opportunities, consolidate tightly-coupled modules, or make a codebase more AI-navigable.
- linear-flow: Use in work repos (github.com/modular, modularml, bentoml) BEFORE responding to any of: substantive work ("help me X", "can you X", "add/create/implement/update/replace/fix Y"), brainstorming / design / planning ("let's brainstorm", "let's design", "let's think about", "let's plan", "how should we", "what do you think about", "what would it take to", "what are our options for", "should we"), explicit Linear mentions ("linear", "the ticket", "the issue", or an issue ID like MOD-1234), or `gh pr create`. ALSO fire BEFORE invoking any planning/design/spec skill — most notably the `brainstorming` skill from the superpowers plugin, but also `writing-plans`, `writing-specs`, or any equivalent. The skill must fire BEFORE the agent starts thinking through the problem — brainstorming first and tracking later is a footgun, because by the time a ticket gets filed the agent has already done unscoped work. Tracks the current Linear issue per Claude session in `~/.claude/linear-sessions/`, suggests existing issues or creates new ones, and injects Linear references into PR bodies with closing vs. non-closing magic words. Skips personal repos (dotfiles, hyprland, emacs, AUR), status-only queries, and quick one-off commands.
- nsys-profile: Profile MAX Serve with NVIDIA Nsight Systems. Launches server with deferred profiling, runs benchmark with --trace to capture nsys profile, and prints stats.
- nsys-profile-k8s: Profile a GPU workload on a Kubernetes node using nsys. Deploys a privileged profiling Pod on the same node as the target, captures a trace, and copies it back locally.
- review-until-clean: Use when the user asks to "review in a loop", "iterate until reviewed clean", "review and resolve until clean twice", or any variant that asks for review→fix cycles to a stable end. Spawns a review subagent that runs the simplify and review skills in series, applies issues, re-reviews — terminates only after TWO consecutive clean reports, then auto-commits and pushes.
- tdd: Use this skill whenever the user wants to write code using TDD, test-driven development, or test-first methodology. Triggers on: "/tdd", "let's do TDD", "write a failing test", "red green refactor", "test-first", "start a TDD cycle", or any request to implement a feature by writing tests before code. Adaptive five-step cycle (RED-DOMAIN-GREEN-DOMAIN-COMMIT) that detects harness capabilities and routes to guided (/tdd red|domain|green|commit) or automated (/tdd) mode. NOT for running existing tests, debugging test failures, or reviewing code -- only for the disciplined test-first cycle.
- upgrade-kadabra-rc: Use when cutting/rolling a new kadabra RC for MiniMax-M3, OR whenever the user asks to update/roll/bump the internal deployment or internal endpoint, watch a modular GitHub Actions image build and then update a deployment, update the MAX serve image, roll M3 to a new build, or deploy the new kadabra/max-internal image. Note: the user often calls this just "the internal deployment"/"the internal endpoint" or frames it as "watch the image build and update the deployment" WITHOUT saying kadabra/minimax/RC — this skill still applies. It tags an RC on max/kadabra-release, builds the internal max-internal image via buildAndPushMAXServeImage, bumps the preview (internal, minimax-org minimax-mxfp8-preview) then customer (minimax-org minimax-m3-mxfp8) MiniMax-M3 endpoints with deployment bump, un-sticks the B200 rollout, and verifies (endpoint regression suite, MiniMax Provider Verifier, llm-fuzz) with failing-request monitoring. Keywords: kadabra, RC, minimax, MiniMax-M3, M3, internal deployment, internal endpoint, preview endpoint, bump, roll, deployment bump, max-internal image, image build, MAX serve, watch the image build, update the deployment, roll M3 to the new build, deploy the new kadabra image.
- explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation of a code change, diff, branch, or PR.
- review-diff: Use when the user wants a rich, annotated review of a code change, diff, branch, or PR — the diff itself organized, annotated, and shown with surrounding codebase context. Complements explain-diff (which teaches); this one is for reviewing.
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- slack:channel-digest: Get a digest of recent activity across multiple Slack channels
- slack:draft-announcement: Draft a well-formatted Slack announcement and save it as a draft
- slack:find-discussions: Find discussions about a specific topic across Slack channels
- slack:standup: Generate a standup update based on your recent Slack activity
- slack:summarize-channel: Summarize recent activity in a Slack channel
- drovr:code-review: Use when you have written any change, before calling it done or handing it forward — including when you are about to review it by some other means, or to ask a human to authorize a reviewer; requires `drovr code-review run` in the foreground, with every Critical and Important finding resolved or explicitly recorded as deferred
- drovr:handoff: Use when finished work in one agent context must be carried across a phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent
- drovr:pipeline: Use when a feature or change is too large for one session and needs a human approval gate on its spec before any code is written
- drovr:systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing or writing a fix — requires a reproduction and a mechanistic root cause before any code change
- drovr:tdd: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code — requires a test you have watched fail before any implementation exists; no production code without a red test first
- drovr:using-drovr: Use at the start of every session and before every response, including before clarifying questions and before reading any file — routes to the right drovr skill and requires invoking it whenever there is even a 1% chance one applies
- drovr:verification-before-completion: Use when about to claim any work is done, fixed, or passing, before reporting, committing, or handing off — requires running the verification command in this message and reading its output; evidence before assertion, always

- slack:block-kit: Help developers build and validate Block Kit layouts for Slack messages, modals, and Home tabs. Provides authoritative block references and validates with the blocks.validate API. Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels). - slack:slack-messaging: Guidance for composing well-formatted, effective Slack messages using standard markdown
- slack:slack-search: Guidance for effectively searching Slack to find messages, files, channels, and people
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. - artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. - keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

content.content:
1	# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols
2	
3	Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.
4	
5	## Load it
6	
7	1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) with the Svalboard plugged in.
8	2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.
9	
10	No reflash — Vial writes the keymap live.
11	
12	Needs `/dev/hidraw*` to be readable, which it isn't by default. The udev rule is
13	in `system/etc/udev/rules.d/92-vial.rules`. Without it, KeyBard and Vial both see
14	the keyboard and then silently fail to open it.
15	
16	## Layers
17	
18	Each finger sits in a cup with five switches: **N**orth, **S**outh, **E**ast,
19	**W**est and **C**enter (the plain down-press). East is screen-right on both
20	hands, so West is inward on the right hand and outward on the left.
21	
22	### Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu
23	
24	```
25	             W    N     C     S     E
26	  L pinky    tab  w     r     x     -
27	  L ring     .    f     s     c     .
28	  L middle   (    m     n     l     v
29	  L index    g    p     t     d     b
30	  R index    ,    .     a     u     :
31	  R middle   /    q     e     o     )
32	  R ring     ;    "     i     y     &
33	  R pinky    z    '     h     k     j
34	```
35	
36	The alphas are Hands Down Neu as it sits on the Glove80 — note `;` on the right
37	inner column where upstream publishes `-`.
38	
39	Two places this departs from a literal port, both because the Svalboard has four
40	fingers per hand and the layout assumes five columns:
41	
42	- **`g` is on the index's West.** Hands Down gives the left index the whole
43	  inner column (`v`/`b`/`g`). Only two fit on an index cup, so it keeps `b` and
44	  `g` and exiles `v` — the rarest — to the middle finger.
45	- **`z`, `j` and `tab` are on laterals.** They live in outer columns the
46	  Svalboard doesn't have. `tab` gets the left pinky's West, x=0.0, the outermost
47	  point of the hand.
48	
49	Brackets are deliberately *not* on this layer; Arensito has them. Five symbols
50	*are*, placed by measured frequency rather than by feel — counted over hand-typed
51	prompts and shell history (agent-driven sessions excluded) and over code authored
52	here, per 1000 characters:
53	
54	| | `-` | `:` | `(` `)` | `&` |
55	|---|---|---|---|---|
56	| code | 11.6 | 9.3 | 4.9 | 0.68 |
57	| hand-typed | 33.5 | 5.1 | 0.30 | 0.17 |
58	
59	- `-` → **left pinky East.** The clear winner on both counts.
60	- `:` → **right index East**, the strongest free lateral. Was shift+`;`.
61	- `(` `)` → **left middle West / right middle East**, an outward-facing mirror
62	  pair, so `()` alternates hands. They earn a base key from code only.
63	- `&` → **right ring East.** The rarest thing on this layer, on the worst key
64	  here, which is the point. Ring laterals are the hardest cups to reach.
65	
66	`*` was considered and rejected: it looks like 6.7/1k in code, but 90% of that
67	is `**` in markdown prose, and it is 0.03/1k in anything hand-typed.
68	
69	Each is promoted, not copied — all five are holes on layer 1, so nothing sits on
70	two keys.
71	
72	### Layer 1 — Arensito symbols (hold `MO(1)`)
73	
74	```
75	  { } [ ] @   · · < > $
76	  ; / · 0 ·   \ 1 · · =
77	  6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
78	```
79	
80	Ported from the Glove80 `symbols` layer. `·` is a dead key — Arensito puts
81	`-`, `:`, `&`, `_`, `(` and `)` there, and all six are one-key elsewhere now
82	(see layer 0 and the thumbs below). They're dead rather than transparent on
83	purpose: falling through would type `n`, `.`, `e`, `i`, `b` and `/` from the
84	middle of the symbol layer.
85	
86	The grid above is on N/C/S; the
87	laterals carry the six symbols Arensito leaves out, which would otherwise cost
88	`MO(1)`+shift+key:
89	
90	```
91	  ` ~ on the left pinky      ! on the left index
92	  % on the left ring         # on the left middle
93	  | on the right index       ^ on the right middle
94	```
95	
96	`?` isn't here on purpose — it's shift+`/`, and `/` is on the base layer.
97	
98	`_` gets a second seat on the **left thumb's space key**. Arensito's own `_` is
99	on the right index's North, the same hand as `MO(1)`; on space it's a
100	left-right roll instead. Space itself isn't typeable while `MO(1)` is held —
101	every other thumb stays transparent, so shift, ctrl, enter and backspace still
102	work on the layer.
103	
104	### Layer 2 — navigation (hold `MO(2)`)
105	
106	Arrows four-across on the right hand, innermost to outermost, matching Glove80
107	base-layer positions 75–78:
108	
109	```
110	  R index  R middle  R ring  R pinky
111	     ←        ↓        ↑        →
112	```
113	
114	F1–F12, home/end, pgup/pgdn, volume and play/pause fill the rest.
115	
116	### Layer 15 — mouse
117	
118	Svalboard's firmware switches here by itself when the pointing device moves, and
119	leaves on the first key that isn't on this layer. **Nothing reaches it by
120	keypress, by design.** Buttons 1/3/2 sit on index/middle/ring South of both
121	hands; `USER06` is `SV_RECALIBRATE_POINTER`.
122	
123	### Thumbs
124	
125	```
126	LEFT                                RIGHT
127	 row7  esc(7.4)  shift(8.5)  ctrl(9.6)     alt(11.4)  MO1(12.5)  MO2(13.6)
128	 row6   space(7.9) delete(9.0) gui(10.1)    enter(11.9) ralt(13.0) bspc(14.1)
129	```
130	
131	The two rows interleave in x, so every row-6 key sits between two row-7 keys —
132	and the **middle** row-6 key on each hand, x=9.0 and x=13.0, is the only
133	position with no free side. Nothing you press in a hurry goes there. `gui` was
134	there originally (on both hands) and was unusable; `tab` was tried there and was
135	worse. They now hold `delete` and `ralt`.
136	
137	`space` left and `bspc` right match Glove80 positions 69 and 74 — Svalboard's own
138	configs ship those mirrored.
139	
140	## Regenerating
141	
142	```sh
143	python3 build.py
144	```
145	
146	`build.py` emits the entire `.vil`. There is no base file to patch and no
147	network access — every layer, keycode and piece of Vial metadata is declared in
148	it. It was cut over from a patch-the-Colemak-config approach by diffing against

# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols

Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.

## Load it

1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) with the Svalboard plugged in.
2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.

No reflash — Vial writes the keymap live.

Needs `/dev/hidraw*` to be readable, which it isn't by default. The udev rule is
in `system/etc/udev/rules.d/92-vial.rules`. Without it, KeyBard and Vial both see
the keyboard and then silently fail to open it.

## Layers

Each finger sits in a cup with five switches: **N**orth, **S**outh, **E**ast,
**W**est and **C**enter (the plain down-press). East is screen-right on both
hands, so West is inward on the right hand and outward on the left.

### Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu

```
             W    N     C     S     E
  L pinky    tab  w     r     x     -
  L ring     .    f     s     c     .
  L middle   (    m     n     l     v
  L index    g    p     t     d     b
  R index    ,    .     a     u     :
  R middle   /    q     e     o     )
  R ring     ;    "     i     y     &
  R pinky    z    '     h     k     j
```

The alphas are Hands Down Neu as it sits on the Glove80 — note `;` on the right
inner column where upstream publishes `-`.

Two places this departs from a literal port, both because the Svalboard has four
fingers per hand and the layout assumes five columns:

- **`g` is on the index's West.** Hands Down gives the left index the whole
  inner column (`v`/`b`/`g`). Only two fit on an index cup, so it keeps `b` and
  `g` and exiles `v` — the rarest — to the middle finger.
- **`z`, `j` and `tab` are on laterals.** They live in outer columns the
  Svalboard doesn't have. `tab` gets the left pinky's West, x=0.0, the outermost
  point of the hand.

Brackets are deliberately *not* on this layer; Arensito has them. Five symbols
*are*, placed by measured frequency rather than by feel — counted over hand-typed
prompts and shell history (agent-driven sessions excluded) and over code authored
here, per 1000 characters:

| | `-` | `:` | `(` `)` | `&` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| code | 11.6 | 9.3 | 4.9 | 0.68 |
| hand-typed | 33.5 | 5.1 | 0.30 | 0.17 |

- `-` → **left pinky East.** The clear winner on both counts.
- `:` → **right index East**, the strongest free lateral. Was shift+`;`.
- `(` `)` → **left middle West / right middle East**, an outward-facing mirror
  pair, so `()` alternates hands. They earn a base key from code only.
- `&` → **right ring East.** The rarest thing on this layer, on the worst key
  here, which is the point. Ring laterals are the hardest cups to reach.

`*` was considered and rejected: it looks like 6.7/1k in code, but 90% of that
is `**` in markdown prose, and it is 0.03/1k in anything hand-typed.

Each is promoted, not copied — all five are holes on layer 1, so nothing sits on
two keys.

### Layer 1 — Arensito symbols (hold `MO(1)`)

```
  { } [ ] @   · · < > $
  ; / · 0 ·   \ 1 · · =
  6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
```

Ported from the Glove80 `symbols` layer. `·` is a dead key — Arensito puts
`-`, `:`, `&`, `_`, `(` and `)` there, and all six are one-key elsewhere now
(see layer 0 and the thumbs below). They're dead rather than transparent on
purpose: falling through would type `n`, `.`, `e`, `i`, `b` and `/` from the
middle of the symbol layer.

The grid above is on N/C/S; the
laterals carry the six symbols Arensito leaves out, which would otherwise cost
`MO(1)`+shift+key:

```
  ` ~ on the left pinky      ! on the left index
  % on the left ring         # on the left middle
  | on the right index       ^ on the right middle
```

`?` isn't here on purpose — it's shift+`/`, and `/` is on the base layer.

`_` gets a second seat on the **left thumb's space key**. Arensito's own `_` is
on the right index's North, the same hand as `MO(1)`; on space it's a
left-right roll instead. Space itself isn't typeable while `MO(1)` is held —
every other thumb stays transparent, so shift, ctrl, enter and backspace still
work on the layer.

### Layer 2 — navigation (hold `MO(2)`)

Arrows four-across on the right hand, innermost to outermost, matching Glove80
base-layer positions 75–78:

```
  R index  R middle  R ring  R pinky
     ←        ↓        ↑        →
```

F1–F12, home/end, pgup/pgdn, volume and play/pause fill the rest.

### Layer 15 — mouse

Svalboard's firmware switches here by itself when the pointing device moves, and
leaves on the first key that isn't on this layer. **Nothing reaches it by
keypress, by design.** Buttons 1/3/2 sit on index/middle/ring South of both
hands; `USER06` is `SV_RECALIBRATE_POINTER`.

### Thumbs

```
LEFT                                RIGHT
 row7  esc(7.4)  shift(8.5)  ctrl(9.6)     alt(11.4)  MO1(12.5)  MO2(13.6)
 row6   space(7.9) delete(9.0) gui(10.1)    enter(11.9) ralt(13.0) bspc(14.1)
```

The two rows interleave in x, so every row-6 key sits between two row-7 keys —
and the **middle** row-6 key on each hand, x=9.0 and x=13.0, is the only
position with no free side. Nothing you press in a hurry goes there. `gui` was
there originally (on both hands) and was unusable; `tab` was tried there and was
worse. They now hold `delete` and `ralt`.

`space` left and `bspc` right match Glove80 positions 69 and 74 — Svalboard's own
configs ship those mirrored.

## Regenerating

```sh
python3 build.py
```

`build.py` emits the entire `.vil`. There is no base file to patch and no
network access — every layer, keycode and piece of Vial metadata is declared in
it. It was cut over from a patch-the-Colemak-config approach by diffing against
the old output until byte-identical, so the rewrite carried nothing over by
accident.

Four guards, any of which aborts the build:

- **Geometry.** `CUP_XY` holds the physical position of all 40 finger switches,
  read out of the keyboard's own `vial.json` over the Vial protocol. The build
  asserts North is above Center, South below, East right and West left, for
  every cup. Get the column order wrong and you still emit a structurally
  perfect file with every key in the wrong place — this is the check that
  catches it, and it checks against the hardware rather than another config's
  conventions.
- **Coverage.** All 26 letters and 10 digits reachable, plus space, backspace,
  enter, tab and grave. Grave has no shift-fallback and went missing once when
  Arensito's `{` landed on top of it.
- **Symbol cost.** No printable ASCII symbol may require `MO(1)`+shift+key.
- **Duplicates.** Nothing on the base layer reachable from two positions.
  Moving a key by adding an override leaves the original behind unless it's
  blanked; that put `g` on two cups once.

Thumb rows are declared by physical x, not column index, and the build fails if
the declared positions don't match the hardware. The indices are **not** mirrored
between hands — left column 3 is at x=7.9 and mirrors right column *4* at
x=13.6, not right column 3 at x=14.1. Reasoning about them directly produced one
wrong answer already.

## Source

Glove80 layout `e3409150-bb22-49c0-8614-10035f3f6a04` ("Sauyon layout
2026-01-20"), layers `Base` and `symbols`. Its grids are transcribed into
`build.py`; nothing is fetched at build time.

Custom `USER*` keycode names (`SV_SCROLL_TOGGLE`, `SV_TOGGLE_AUTOMOUSE`, the
sniper modes, DPI controls) come from the keyboard itself — Vial command
`0xFE 0x02` returns an LZMA-compressed `vial.json` describing them.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Generate a Svalboard Vial keymap (.vil) for Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols.
3	
4	Emits the whole file. There is no base .vil to patch and no network access --
5	every layer, every keycode and all the Vial metadata is declared below.
6	
7	Source of truth for the alphas and symbols is my Glove80, my.glove80.com layout
8	e3409150-bb22-49c0-8614-10035f3f6a04, layers `Base` and `symbols`. Its grids are
9	transcribed into the constants below.
10	
11	Run `python3 build.py` to write SvalHandsDownNeu.vil. The build refuses to emit
12	anything unless check_geometry() and check_coverage() both pass.
13	"""
14	
15	import json
16	import pathlib
17	import sys
18	
19	HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
20	OUT = HERE / "SvalHandsDownNeu.vil"
21	
22	# uid identifies the physical keyboard. Read off mine over the Vial protocol
23	# (raw HID usage page 0xFF60, command 0xFE 0x00). Vial warns on a mismatch.
24	UID = 5199957870438586395
25	
26	LAYERS = 16
27	ROWS = 10
28	COLS = 6
29	
30	# --- Svalboard geometry ------------------------------------------------------
31	#
32	# layout[layer] is 10 rows x 6 columns.
33	#
34	#   row 0 = left thumb cluster      row 5 = right thumb cluster
35	#   rows 1-4 = left  index, middle, ring, pinky
36	#   rows 6-9 = right index, middle, ring, pinky
37	#
38	# A finger row's first five columns are the five switches of that cup, in
39	# absolute directions -- East is screen-right on both hands. Column 5 is unused
40	# on finger rows and must be -1; thumb rows use all six.
41	
42	S, E, C, N, W = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
43	
44	L_THUMB, R_THUMB = 0, 5
45	L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY = 1, 2, 3, 4
46	R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY = 6, 7, 8, 9
47	
48	THUMB_ROWS = (L_THUMB, R_THUMB)
49	FINGER_ROWS = (L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY,
50	               R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY)
51	
52	FINGER_NAMES = {
53	    L_INDEX: "L index", L_MIDDLE: "L middle", L_RING: "L ring", L_PINKY: "L pinky",
54	    R_INDEX: "R index", R_MIDDLE: "R middle", R_RING: "R ring", R_PINKY: "R pinky",
55	}
56	DIR_NAMES = {S: "South", E: "East", C: "Center", N: "North", W: "West"}
57	
58	# Physical key positions, in KLE units, read out of the keyboard's own vial.json
59	# (Vial command 0xFE 0x02, LZMA-compressed). This is the hardware's account of
60	# itself, not a convention borrowed from some other config -- which is what
61	# makes check_geometry() below worth running.
62	CUP_XY = {
63	    L_INDEX:  {S: (9.5, 3.5),  E: (10.5, 2.5), C: (9.5, 2.5),  N: (9.5, 1.5),  W: (8.5, 2.5)},
64	    L_MIDDLE: {S: (7.0, 2.0),  E: (8.0, 1.0),  C: (7.0, 1.0),  N: (7.0, 0.0),  W: (6.0, 1.0)},
65	    L_RING:   {S: (3.5, 2.0),  E: (4.5, 1.0),  C: (3.5, 1.0),  N: (3.5, 0.0),  W: (2.5, 1.0)},
66	    L_PINKY:  {S: (1.0, 3.5),  E: (2.0, 2.5),  C: (1.0, 2.5),  N: (1.0, 1.5),  W: (0.0, 2.5)},
67	    R_INDEX:  {S: (14.5, 3.5), E: (15.5, 2.5), C: (14.5, 2.5), N: (14.5, 1.5), W: (13.5, 2.5)},
68	    R_MIDDLE: {S: (17.0, 2.0), E: (18.0, 1.0), C: (17.0, 1.0), N: (17.0, 0.0), W: (16.0, 1.0)},
69	    R_RING:   {S: (20.5, 2.0), E: (21.5, 1.0), C: (20.5, 1.0), N: (20.5, 0.0), W: (19.5, 1.0)},
70	    R_PINKY:  {S: (23.0, 3.5), E: (24.0, 2.5), C: (23.0, 2.5), N: (23.0, 1.5), W: (22.0, 2.5)},
71	}
72	
73	# Thumb keys, same source. Reason about these by x, never by column index -- the
74	# indices are NOT mirrored between hands (left col 3 at x=7.9 is the mirror of
75	# right col 4 at x=13.6, not right col 3 at x=14.1).
76	THUMB_XY = {
77	    L_THUMB: {4: (7.4, 7.0), 3: (7.9, 6.0), 2: (8.5, 7.0),
78	              5: (9.0, 6.0), 0: (9.6, 7.0), 1: (10.1, 6.0)},
79	    R_THUMB: {0: (11.4, 7.0), 1: (11.9, 6.0), 2: (12.5, 7.0),
80	              5: (13.0, 6.0), 4: (13.6, 7.0), 3: (14.1, 6.0)},
81	}
82	
83	# --- Alpha block placement ---------------------------------------------------
84	#
85	# A layout's alpha block is 3 rows x 5 columns, written the way layouts always
86	# are: outward-in on the left hand, inward-out on the right.
87	#
88	#   left:  pinky ring middle index inner      right: inner index middle ring pinky
89	#
90	# The Svalboard has four fingers per hand and no inner-index column, so the
91	# inner column spills onto one inward-facing lateral per finger. That lateral is
92	# East on the left hand and West on the right.
93	
94	INNER_LATERAL = {"top": "middle", "home": "index", "bottom": "ring"}
95	
96	
97	def place(block, hand):
98	    """Map a 3x5 alpha block onto {(row, col): keycode} for one hand."""
99	    if hand == "left":
100	        rows = {"pinky": L_PINKY, "ring": L_RING, "middle": L_MIDDLE, "index": L_INDEX}
101	        cols = ["pinky", "ring", "middle", "index"]
102	        inner_col, lateral = 4, E
103	    else:
104	        rows = {"pinky": R_PINKY, "ring": R_RING, "middle": R_MIDDLE, "index": R_INDEX}
105	        cols = ["index", "middle", "ring", "pinky"]
106	        inner_col, lateral = 0, W
107	
108	    out = {}
109	    for i, finger in enumerate(cols):
110	        col = i if hand == "left" else i + 1
111	        out[(rows[finger], N)] = block["top"][col]
112	        out[(rows[finger], C)] = block["home"][col]
113	        out[(rows[finger], S)] = block["bottom"][col]
114	
115	    for band, finger in INNER_LATERAL.items():
116	        out[(rows[finger], lateral)] = block[band][inner_col]
117	
118	    return out
119	
120	
121	# --- Layer 0: Hands Down Neu -------------------------------------------------
122	#
123	#   w f m p v   / . q " ' z
124	#   r s n t b   , a e i h j
125	#   x c l d g   ; u o y k
126	#
127	# As it sits on the Glove80, including `;` on the right inner column where
128	# upstream Hands Down Neu publishes `-`.
129	
130	HDNEU_LEFT = {
131	    "top":    ["KC_W", "KC_F", "KC_M", "KC_P", "KC_V"],
132	    "home":   ["KC_R", "KC_S", "KC_N", "KC_T", "KC_B"],
133	    "bottom": ["KC_X", "KC_C", "KC_L", "KC_D", "KC_G"],
134	}
135	
136	HDNEU_RIGHT = {
137	    "top":    ["KC_SLASH", "KC_DOT", "KC_Q", "LSFT(KC_QUOTE)", "KC_QUOTE"],
138	    "home":   ["KC_COMMA", "KC_A", "KC_E", "KC_I", "KC_H"],
139	    "bottom": ["KC_SCOLON", "KC_U", "KC_O", "KC_Y", "KC_K"],
140	}
141	
142	# The Glove80's outer column (z, j) and its bottom row (grave, backslash,
143	# brackets) have no Svalboard equivalent -- those are columns this keyboard
144	# doesn't have. They go on the spare laterals, openers left and closers right.
145	BASE_LATERALS = {
146	    (R_PINKY, W): "KC_Z",    # inner, x=22.0
147	    (R_PINKY, E): "KC_J",    # outer, x=24.0
148	    # Hands Down Neu publishes `-` on the right inner column; this port puts `;`
149	    # there, following the Glove80. That evicts `-`, and `-` is far too frequent
150	    # -- kebab-case, `->`, `--flag` -- to sit behind MO(1). It gets a lateral.
151	    (L_PINKY, E): "KC_MINUS",
152	    (L_PINKY, W): "KC_TAB",    # outermost key on the left hand, x=0.0
153	
154	    # Parens likewise: frequent enough in code to be worth a base-layer key
155	    # rather than MO(1)+key.
156	    #
157	    # They were on the left ring's two laterals, which is the wrong pair. The
158	    # ring laterals are the hardest keys on this board to hit -- that is a
159	    # verdict from typing on it, and the only kind available: CUP_XY is KLE
160	    # layout units, so it can say where a key is drawn but nothing about the
161	    # reach. Nothing frequent goes on a ring lateral.
162	    #
163	    # The middles' outer laterals are the strongest free pair instead, and they
164	    # mirror: West is outward on the left hand, East outward on the right. That
165	    # also makes `()` alternate hands rather than roll along one.
166	    (L_MIDDLE, W): "LSFT(KC_9)",
167	    (R_MIDDLE, E): "LSFT(KC_0)",
168	
169	    # `:` takes the index's East, the strongest free right-hand lateral. It is
170	    # the most frequent symbol that still costs two keys: ~9 per 1000 chars of
171	    # code written here, and that survives context-checking -- 47% of it is
172	    # `key: value` in yaml/json/nix and 16% slices and ternaries, against only
173	    # 27% prose colon. It was shift+`;`, so this saves one keystroke, the same
174	    # win the parens got.
175	    (R_INDEX, E): "LSFT(KC_SCOLON)",
176	
177	    # `&` is the opposite case and lands on a ring lateral deliberately: 0.68
178	    # per 1000 in code, 0.17 in hand-typed text, the rarest thing on the base
179	    # layer. The ring laterals are the worst keys here, which is exactly what a

191	    # letters and only v -- the rarest -- is exiled to the middle finger:
192	    #

194	    #
195	    (L_INDEX, W): "KC_G",

199	    (L_RING, E): "KC_NO",

201	
202	# Thumb clusters, declared by physical x rather than column index -- the indices

205	#
206	# The cluster is two interleaved rows: y=7.0 at x 7.4/8.5/9.6 (left) and

216	# GUI used to sit on both x=9.0 and x=13.0, i.e. both unreachable slots, which

219	#
220	# The two flanked slots get keys you genuinely never need in a hurry. Tab was

225	# actually lives (position 22). Delete takes x=9.0 in its place; the Glove80
226	# also has Delete on a thumb (55). RALT takes x=13.0, likewise from the Glove80
227	# right thumb (72).
228	BASE_L_THUMB_X = {
229	    7.4: "KC_ESCAPE",
230	    7.9: "KC_SPACE",
231	    8.5: "KC_LSHIFT",
232	    9.0: "KC_DELETE",   # flanked both sides -- nothing time-critical here
233	    9.6: "KC_LCTRL",
234	    10.1: "KC_LGUI",
235	}
236	
237	BASE_R_THUMB_X = {
238	    11.4: "KC_LALT",
239	    11.9: "KC_ENTER",
240	    12.5: "MO(1)",
241	    13.0: "KC_RALT",    # flanked both sides
242	    13.6: "MO(2)",
243	    14.1: "KC_BSPACE",
244	}

247	def thumb_row(by_x, row):
248	    """Turn an {x: keycode} thumb declaration into column order."""
249	    x_to_col = {xy[0]: col for col, xy in THUMB_XY[row].items()}
250	    if set(by_x) != set(x_to_col):
251	        raise SystemExit(
252	            f"thumb row {row}: declared x positions {sorted(by_x)} do not match "
253	            f"the hardware's {sorted(x_to_col)}"
254	        )
255	    cells = [None] * COLS
256	    for x, code in by_x.items():
257	        cells[x_to_col[x]] = code
258	    return cells

260	
261	def thumb_col(row, x):
262	    """Column index of the thumb key at physical x, for sparse overrides."""
263	    for col, xy in THUMB_XY[row].items():
264	        if xy[0] == x:
265	            return col
266	    raise SystemExit(
267	        f"thumb row {row}: no key at x={x}, hardware has "
268	        f"{sorted(xy[0] for xy in THUMB_XY[row].values())}"
269	    )
270	
271	# --- Layer 1: Arensito symbols ----------------------------------------------
272	#
273	#   { } [ ] @   & _ < > $
274	#   ; / - 0 :   \ 1 ( ) =
275	#   6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
276	#
277	# Ported from the Glove80 `symbols` layer, reached there by a sticky `&sl 3`
278	# and here by holding MO(1) on the right thumb.
279	
280	# Six of Arensito's own cells are holes here. Each of those symbols is already
281	# reachable in one key elsewhere, and nothing should be on two keys:
282	#
283	#   `-`     base layer, left pinky East          -- no MO(1) at all
284	#   `(` `)` base layer, left/right middle outer  -- no MO(1) at all
285	#   `:`     base layer, right index East         -- no MO(1) at all
286	#   `&`     base layer, right ring East          -- no MO(1) at all
287	#   `_`     left thumb's space key               -- see SYMBOL_THUMB_X below
288	#
289	# They are KC_NO rather than KC_TRNS on purpose. Transparent would fall through
290	# to layer 0 and quietly type `n`, `.`, `e`, `i`, `b` and `/` from the middle of
291	# the symbol layer; a dead key is the lesser failure.
292	ARENSITO_LEFT = {
293	    "top":    ["LSFT(KC_LBRACKET)", "LSFT(KC_RBRACKET)", "KC_LBRACKET", "KC_RBRACKET", "LSFT(KC_2)"],
294	    "home":   ["KC_SCOLON", "KC_SLASH", "KC_NO", "KC_0", "KC_NO"],   # were `-` `:`
295	    "bottom": ["KC_6", "KC_7", "KC_8", "KC_9", "LSFT(KC_EQUAL)"],
296	}
297	
298	ARENSITO_RIGHT = {
299	    "top":    ["KC_NO", "KC_NO", "LSFT(KC_COMMA)", "LSFT(KC_DOT)", "LSFT(KC_4)"],   # were `&` `_`
300	    "home":   ["KC_BSLASH", "KC_1", "KC_NO", "KC_NO", "KC_EQUAL"],   # were `(` `)`
301	    "bottom": ["LSFT(KC_8)", "KC_2", "KC_3", "KC_4", "KC_5"],
302	}
303	
304	# Arensito uses no lateral on the left pinky, and grave has to live somewhere:
305	# it is on the Glove80's base layer and `!#%^` stay reachable as shift+digit
306	# only because this layer carries all ten digits. Grave has no such fallback.
307	# Arensito's own grid covers most of ASCII, but ! # % ^ | ~ are only reachable
308	# as shift+digit or shift+backslash -- and since the digits and backslash are
309	# themselves on this layer, that means holding MO(1) AND shift AND the key.
310	# Three keys for `!` is not a symbol layer doing its job. They go on the laterals
311	# Arensito leaves free, paired with their unshifted partners where that helps:
312	# ~ beside `, | beside \.
313	#
314	# `?` is deliberately absent: it is shift+/ and `/` is on the base layer, so it
315	# already costs two keys, not three.
316	SYMBOL_LATERALS = {
317	    (L_PINKY, W): "KC_GRAVE",
318	    (L_PINKY, E): "LSFT(KC_GRAVE)",    # ~  beside `
319	    (L_INDEX, W): "LSFT(KC_1)",        # !  easiest left lateral, most frequent
320	    (L_MIDDLE, W): "LSFT(KC_3)",       # #
321	    (L_RING, W): "LSFT(KC_5)",         # %
322	    (R_INDEX, E): "LSFT(KC_BSLASH)",   # |  beside \ on the index's West
323	    (R_MIDDLE, E): "LSFT(KC_6)",       # ^
324	}
325	
326	# `_` also takes the left thumb's space key. Arensito puts it on the right
327	# index's North, which is the same hand as MO(1) on the right thumb -- so
328	# snake_case is a same-hand contortion. On space it is MO(1) right, `_` left,
329	# the same alternating roll as any other layer-1 symbol. `_` stays on the right
330	# index too; this is a second seat, not a move.
331	#
332	# The cost is that space is not typeable while MO(1) is held. Every other thumb
333	# stays transparent, so shift, ctrl, enter and backspace all still work on the
334	# layer. Declared by x like the base thumbs, for the reason in BASE_L_THUMB_X.
335	SYMBOL_THUMB_X = {
336	    L_THUMB: {7.9: "LSFT(KC_MINUS)"},
337	}
338	
339	# --- Layer 2: navigation and function keys -----------------------------------
340	#
341	# Arrows four-across on the right hand, matching Glove80 base-layer positions
342	# 75-78 (LEFT DOWN UP RIGHT), innermost to outermost. The Svalboard has no spare
343	# row for them, hence a layer.
344	
345	NAV = {
346	    (L_PINKY, N): "KC_F1", (L_PINKY, C): "KC_HOME", (L_PINKY, S): "KC_F9",
347	    (L_RING, N): "KC_F2", (L_RING, C): "KC_END", (L_RING, S): "KC_F10",
348	    (L_MIDDLE, N): "KC_F3", (L_MIDDLE, S): "KC_PSCREEN",
349	    (L_INDEX, N): "KC_F4", (L_INDEX, S): "KC_MPLY",
350	
351	    (R_INDEX, N): "KC_F5", (R_INDEX, C): "KC_LEFT", (R_INDEX, S): "KC_VOLU",
352	    (R_MIDDLE, N): "KC_F6", (R_MIDDLE, C): "KC_DOWN", (R_MIDDLE, S): "KC_VOLD",
353	    (R_RING, N): "KC_F7", (R_RING, C): "KC_UP", (R_RING, S): "KC_F11",
354	    (R_RING, E): "KC_PGUP",
355	    (R_PINKY, N): "KC_F8", (R_PINKY, C): "KC_RIGHT", (R_PINKY, S): "KC_F12",
356	    (R_PINKY, E): "KC_PGDOWN",
357	}
358	
359	# --- Layer 15: mouse ---------------------------------------------------------
360	#
361	# Svalboard's firmware switches to layer 15 by itself when the pointing device
362	# moves, and leaves on the first key that isn't on it -- there is deliberately
363	# no key that reaches this layer. USER06 is SV_RECALIBRATE_POINTER (the custom
364	# keycode names come from the keyboard's own vial.json).
365	
366	MOUSE = {
367	    (L_INDEX, S): "KC_BTN1", (L_MIDDLE, S): "KC_BTN3", (L_RING, S): "KC_BTN2",
368	    (L_PINKY, C): "USER06",
369	    (R_INDEX, S): "KC_BTN1", (R_MIDDLE, S): "KC_BTN3", (R_RING, S): "KC_BTN2",
370	    (R_PINKY, C): "USER06",
371	}
372	
373	
374	def blank_layer(fill):
375	    """A 10x6 layer of `fill`, with column 5 held at -1 on the finger rows."""
376	    layer = []
377	    for row in range(ROWS):
378	        if row in THUMB_ROWS:
379	            layer.append([fill] * COLS)
380	        else:
381	            layer.append([fill] * (COLS - 1) + [-1])
382	    return layer
383	
384	
385	def build_layers():
386	    layers = [blank_layer("KC_NO") for _ in range(LAYERS)]
387	
388	    # Layer 0 -- alphas, laterals, thumbs.
389	    base = {}
390	    base.update(place(HDNEU_LEFT, "left"))
391	    base.update(place(HDNEU_RIGHT, "right"))
392	    base.update(BASE_LATERALS)
393	    for (row, col), code in base.items():
394	        layers[0][row][col] = code
395	    layers[0][L_THUMB] = thumb_row(BASE_L_THUMB_X, L_THUMB)
396	    layers[0][R_THUMB] = thumb_row(BASE_R_THUMB_X, R_THUMB)
397	
398	    # Layers 1, 2 and 15 fall through to layer 0 wherever they define nothing.
399	    for index, table in ((1, {}), (2, {}), (15, {})):
400	        layers[index] = blank_layer("KC_TRNS")
401	
402	    sym = {}
403	    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_LEFT, "left"))
404	    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_RIGHT, "right"))
405	    sym.update(SYMBOL_LATERALS)
406	    for (row, col), code in sym.items():
407	        layers[1][row][col] = code
408	    for row, by_x in SYMBOL_THUMB_X.items():
409	        for x, code in by_x.items():
410	            layers[1][row][thumb_col(row, x)] = code
411	
412	    # Arensito covers every finger cup except the laterals; anything it leaves
413	    # alone should fall through rather than repeat layer 0's brackets.
414	    for (row, col), code in NAV.items():
415	        layers[2][row][col] = code
416	    for row in FINGER_ROWS:
417	        for col in (S, E, C, N, W):
418	            if (row, col) not in NAV:
419	                layers[2][row][col] = "KC_NO"
420	
421	    for (row, col), code in MOUSE.items():
422	        layers[15][row][col] = code
423	
424	    return layers
425	
426	
427	def check_geometry():
428	    """Verify S/E/C/N/W against the hardware's own coordinates.
429	
430	    This is the check that matters. Everything else in this file assumes column
431	    0 is South, 1 East, 2 Center, 3 North, 4 West -- get that wrong and the
432	    build still emits a structurally perfect .vil with every key in the wrong
433	    place. CUP_XY comes from the keyboard, so the assertion is against physical
434	    reality rather than against another config's conventions.
435	    """
436	    bad = []
437	    for row, dirs in CUP_XY.items():
438	        name = FINGER_NAMES[row]
439	        cx, cy = dirs[C]
440	        checks = [
441	            ("North above Center", dirs[N][1] < cy and dirs[N][0] == cx),
442	            ("South below Center", dirs[S][1] > cy and dirs[S][0] == cx),
443	            ("East right of Center", dirs[E][0] > cx and dirs[E][1] == cy),
444	            ("West left of Center", dirs[W][0] < cx and dirs[W][1] == cy),
445	        ]
446	        for label, ok in checks:
447	            if not ok:
448	                bad.append(f"  {name}: {label} -- got {dirs}")
449	
450	    if bad:
451	        raise SystemExit("geometry check FAILED:\n" + "\n".join(bad))
452	    return len(CUP_XY) * 4
453	
454	
455	def check_coverage(layers):
456	    """Every letter typeable, every digit typeable, nothing silently missing."""
457	    present = {k for lay in layers for row in lay for k in row if isinstance(k, str)}
458	
459	    missing = [c for c in "REDACTED"
460	               if f"KC_{c.upper()}" not in present]
461	    if missing:
462	        raise SystemExit(f"coverage FAILED -- letters unreachable: {missing}")
463	
464	    digits = [d for d in "0123456789" if f"KC_{d}" not in present]
465	    if digits:
466	        raise SystemExit(f"coverage FAILED -- digits unreachable: {digits}")
467	
468	    # Grave has no shift-reachable fallback the way !#%^ do; it went missing
469	    # once already when Arensito's `{` landed on top of it.
470	    for code in ("KC_GRAVE", "KC_SPACE", "KC_BSPACE", "KC_ENTER", "KC_TAB"):
471	        if code not in present:
472	            raise SystemExit(f"coverage FAILED -- {code} is on no layer")
473	
474	    # Every printable ASCII symbol should cost at most two keys: a direct
475	    # keycode somewhere, or shift plus a base-layer key. Anything needing
476	    # MO(1)+shift+key is a three-key combo and counts as missing.
477	    DIRECT = {
478	        "!": "LSFT(KC_1)", '"': "LSFT(KC_QUOTE)", "#": "LSFT(KC_3)",
479	        "$": "LSFT(KC_4)", "%": "LSFT(KC_5)", "&": "LSFT(KC_7)",
480	        "'": "KC_QUOTE", "(": "LSFT(KC_9)", ")": "LSFT(KC_0)",
481	        "*": "LSFT(KC_8)", "+": "LSFT(KC_EQUAL)", ",": "KC_COMMA",
482	        "-": "KC_MINUS", ".": "KC_DOT", "/": "KC_SLASH",
483	        ":": "LSFT(KC_SCOLON)", ";": "KC_SCOLON", "<": "LSFT(KC_COMMA)",
484	        "=": "KC_EQUAL", ">": "LSFT(KC_DOT)", "?": "LSFT(KC_SLASH)",
485	        "@": "LSFT(KC_2)", "[": "KC_LBRACKET", "\\": "KC_BSLASH",
486	        "]": "KC_RBRACKET", "^": "LSFT(KC_6)", "_": "LSFT(KC_MINUS)",
487	        "`": "KC_GRAVE", "{": "LSFT(KC_LBRACKET)", "|": "LSFT(KC_BSLASH)",
488	        "}": "LSFT(KC_RBRACKET)", "~": "LSFT(KC_GRAVE)",
489	    }
490	    base_codes = {k for row in layers[0] for k in row if isinstance(k, str)}
491	    costly = []
492	    for char, code in sorted(DIRECT.items()):
493	        if code in present:
494	            continue
495	        # shift + a base-layer key is fine; shift + a layer-1 key is not
496	        if code.startswith("LSFT(") and code[5:-1] in base_codes:
497	            continue
498	        costly.append(char)
499	    if costly:
500	        raise SystemExit(
501	            "symbol FAILED -- these cost MO(1)+shift+key: " + " ".join(costly)
502	        )
503	
504	    # Moving a key by adding an override leaves the original in place unless it
505	    # is explicitly blanked -- that is how `g` briefly ended up on two cups.
506	    # Nothing on the base layer should be reachable from two positions.
507	    seen = {}
508	    for row, cells in enumerate(layers[0]):
509	        for col, code in enumerate(cells):
510	            if not isinstance(code, str) or code in ("KC_NO", "KC_TRNS"):
511	                continue
512	            if code in seen:
513	                raise SystemExit(
514	                    f"duplicate FAILED -- {code} is on base layer at "
515	                    f"{seen[code]} and again at (row {row}, col {col})"
516	                )
517	            seen[code] = f"(row {row}, col {col})"
518	
519	    for index, layer in enumerate(layers):
520	        if len(layer) != ROWS:
521	            raise SystemExit(f"layer {index} has {len(layer)} rows, want {ROWS}")
522	        for row, cells in enumerate(layer):
523	            if len(cells) != COLS:
524	                raise SystemExit(f"layer {index} row {row} has {len(cells)} cols")
525	            if row not in THUMB_ROWS and cells[5] != -1:
526	                raise SystemExit(
527	                    f"layer {index} row {row} col 5 is {cells[5]!r}, must be -1 "
528	                    "on finger rows"
529	                )
530	    return len(present)
531	
532	
533	def main():
534	    checked = check_geometry()
535	    print(f"geometry OK: {checked} direction assertions against the hardware")
536	
537	    layers = build_layers()
538	    distinct = check_coverage(layers)
539	    print(f"coverage OK: 26 letters, 10 digits, {distinct} distinct keycodes")
540	
541	    vil = {
542	        "version": 1,
543	        "uid": UID,
544	        "layout": layers,
545	        "encoder_layout": [[] for _ in range(LAYERS)],
546	        "layout_options": -1,
547	        "macro": [[] for _ in range(50)],
548	        "vial_protocol": 6,
549	        "via_protocol": 9,
550	        "tap_dance": [["KC_NO", "KC_NO", "KC_NO", "KC_NO", 200] for _ in range(50)],
551	        "combo": [["KC_NO"] * 5 for _ in range(50)],
552	        "key_override": [
553	            {
554	                "trigger": "KC_NO",
555	                "replacement": "KC_NO",
556	                "layers": 65535,
557	                "trigger_mods": 0,
558	                "negative_mod_mask": 0,
559	                "suppressed_mods": 0,
560	                "options": 7,
561	            }
562	            for _ in range(10)
563	        ],
564	        # Svalboard's QMK settings, as read off the keyboard. Vial writes these
565	        # back verbatim; they are timings and pointer tuning, not key positions.
566	        "settings": {
567	            "1": 0, "2": 50, "3": 0, "4": 175, "5": 5, "6": 5000, "7": 200,
568	            "8": 0, "9": 150, "10": 60, "11": 8, "12": 5, "13": 7, "14": 10,
569	            "15": 80, "16": 8, "17": 40, "18": 0, "19": 80, "20": 5, "21": 128,
570	        },
571	    }
572	
573	    OUT.write_text(json.dumps(vil, indent=2) + "\n")
574	    live = sum(1 for lay in layers for row in lay for k in row
575	               if isinstance(k, str) and k not in ("KC_NO", "KC_TRNS"))
576	    print(f"wrote {OUT.name}: {LAYERS} layers, {live} live keys")
577	
578	
579	if __name__ == "__main__":
580	    sys.exit(main())
